content:
**Subject and central claims.** This section continues Steven Pinker's account of vision climbing from the retinal sketch toward abstract thought, focusing on how shapes get recognized and how reference frames make perception possible. On file page 157 (printed 267–268), drawing on Irvin Rock and Fred Attneave, Pinker argues that perceived shape depends on an imposed frame: a square and a diamond are geometrically identical, differing only in alignment to the viewer's up-down axis, and Attneave's triangles flip "which way they point" as symmetry axes take turns dominating. Frames can come from objects themselves and tend to embrace whole neighborhoods of shapes.

**Shape recognition as the core problem.** File page 158 (printed 268–270) states the difficulty: adults name roughly ten thousand things, mostly by shape, and a moved object changes its 2½-D sketch, so a stored copy of that sketch would fail to match. Pinker presents David Marr's solution: memory stores shape in an object-centered frame, aligned to axes of elongation and symmetry, with parts positioned relative to the object ("handle parallel to the edge of the slab"), and matching uses forgiving categories rather than pixel comparison. File page 159 (printed 270–271) adds Irvin Biederman's "geons": about twenty-four simple solids joined by attachment relations ("above," "beside," "end to end") defined in the object's frame. Geons are explicitly combinatorial like grammar — arrangement matters (cylinder plus side elbow is a cup; top elbow is a pail), and a small vocabulary yields millions of objects. Pinker notes a neurological patient whose left-hemisphere stroke fragmented imagined part arrangements, while the right hemisphere measures whole shapes. He claims geon descriptions also support understanding what objects are for, not just naming them.

**Aesthetics and limits of geons.** File page 160 (printed 272–273) quotes Quentin Bell: clothing lets the mind infer idealized, more perfect forms, omitting dents and irregularities, consistent with geon idealization. But geons fail for fractal natural objects (mountains, trees become pyramids and lollipops) and cannot individuate particular faces across expression and aging. Pinker reviews prosopagnosia (patient "LH" lost face identity but kept object recognition) and a contrasting patient with object-recognition trouble but intact face recognition, arguing face recognition is distinct, not merely harder.

**Disagreement and refinement.** File page 161 (printed 273–275) records Pinker's own qualification: a "face module" is really a module tuned to particular geometries (distances between symmetrical blobs, curvature over a 3-D skeleton), so it will process nonfaces sharing those features. He then stresses geon theory is not true in pure form: opacity means no single view-independent description is possible; Marr ignored surfaces, Biederman stores several view-specific geon models. This opens alternatives — many view files with a pattern-associator network interpolating (forty views at most, per recent work), or mental rotation. File page 162 (printed 276–277) reports Lynn Cooper and Roger Shepard: reaction time for judging normal versus mirror-reversed letters rose with misorientation, a signature of mental rotation. But Pinker cautions that mirror-image discrimination is special (handedness of hands, molecules, and even cobalt-60 decay), so the experiment does not settle ordinary recognition.

**Engineering implications (mine, not Pinker's).** For an inspectable non-neural machine, the section suggests: represent objects in object-centered frames with parts and attachment relations; use categorical, tolerance-bearing descriptors rather than exact molds; permit multiple view-indexed representations plus a rotation operator; and treat reference frames as first-class structures that can be selected, grouped, and switched. The permitted scope of a rule (relations invariant under motion) must be distinguished from memorized exemplars (view files). Innate capacities here are the frame-forming and geometry-sensitive mechanisms; acquired knowledge is the catalog of geon assemblies, names, and views. The section leaves unsolved how parts are segmented from the 2½-D sketch, how frames are chosen when ambiguous, how recognition feeds reasoning, goals, memory over time, causation, analogy, or emotion — none of which are treated here. The square/diamond and Attneave demonstrations are visually dependent; the geon counts and the "forty views" figure are reported claims, not verified here. Narrow results (Cooper–Shepard rotation, Biederman's inventory) should not be read as universal learning laws.
